Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Industry observers note that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Industry observers note that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

It has been revealed that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Industry observers note that leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

In a recent development, there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data highlights him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

It has been revealed that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

In a recent development, A recent study showed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

It has been revealed that there is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper claims that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

Industry observers note that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

Recent findings suggest that in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

It has been revealed that he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

Recent findings suggest that it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

According to recent reports, clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

According to recent reports, as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

In a recent development, the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In a recent development, in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Recent findings suggest that chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

The other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

Sources indicate that the three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Sources indicate that later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

It has been revealed that he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

It has been revealed that clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

Industry observers note that if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how big they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

Recent findings suggest that his 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

Sources indicate that in fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

Industry observers note that on Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

Recent findings suggest that it is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

The area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Sources indicate that the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

In a recent development, I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary Upcoming Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

In a recent development, the real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he highlights to the world.”.

Andrew Skurka on Pro Tips for Older Hikers

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service.
  • If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. In my 20s, I was a dirtbag thru-hiker. I was the first person to do the C2C Route, the Great Western Loop, and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition.

Industry observers note that for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service. Every year, I get to go to places like southern Utah, Alaska, Yellowstone, and the High Sierra to teach other people backpacking skills.

If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.

And if you’re looking to have an exceptional backpacking experience in 2027, please consider joining me on one of my guided backpacking trips. We are accepting applications starting Monday, December 7th, 2026. For more information, you can learn more here.

Today’s video is geared toward backpackers who are getting up there in age. I’m going to help set your expectations about what’s to come and also give you ideas about how to keep backpacking fun late into life.

In a recent development, now, importantly, I should mention I’m not old at 45, but I do work with a lot of older backpackers. And I think what’s fair to say, too, is that at 45, I’ve been backpacking for over half my life, since 21.

And backpacking for me has changed as I’ve gotten older, and I expect that it will continue to change as I get into my 50s and 60s and 70s.

In some respects, backpacking gets easier as you get older. So specifically, you tend to have more money, you have more time, and you’re probably more motivated because you know that the window of opportunity is closing.

But mostly, for backpackers who are getting older, the key takeaway should be that backpacking is going to get harder physically.

Industry observers note that putting in those miles, hiking all that vertical, trying to recover overnight, sleeping on the ground—none of that gets easier as you get into your 50s, 60s, and 70s. It was much easier when you were in your sprightly 20s and 30s.

Industry observers note that so the key thing that I would say to an older backpacker is, what are you going to do? Are you going to stop backpacking? Or are you going to make some adaptations and some tweaks to your approach to make sure that you can keep backpacking late into life?

Photo courtesy of Andrew Skurka.

Let me put this conversation into context by giving you some statistics from our guided trip program.

So every year, we have about 400 to 500 clients on our trips. And I’ll give you some specific data from 2026, although these patterns haven’t changed a lot in many years.

In 2026, 24% of our clients were in their 50s, 23% of our clients were in their 60s, and only 4% of our clients were in their 70s.

Industry observers note that I’m not in my 70s, but I do have 70-year-old parents and 70-year-old in-laws. I don’t want to speculate about what might be happening in the 70s that’s responsible for that significant drop-off.

But to anyone who’s approaching this phase of life, this empty-nester, retiree stage of life, just realize that the window will close.

So if you have goals, if you have backpacking goals, just make sure not to wait too long on them because as you get older and older, backpacking definitely seems to get more difficult and participation rates go down.

There are certainly exceptions to these demographic trends that I just gave you.

I would call out, for example, Greybeard, who at 91 just became the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. But he’s a freak. He’s a total freak. He’s such an outlier.

For the average backpacker, for the average person, I would expect that your backpacking interests will fade during your 60s or into your early 70s.

Let’s talk about the physical challenges of backpacking and how you can mitigate or adapt to them.

As we get older, the first reckoning is that putting in the same amount of miles and the same amount of vertical that we did when we were younger just gets harder.

You can push into it, but you’re not going to recover as quickly, and the time it takes you to do those miles and that vertical is going to be longer, which cuts into camp time.

So you might not like the solution, but I just think it’s realistic: You need to start planning less ambitious itineraries.

Relatedly, but it’s a little bit more specific, one thing that we really observe with our older clients is a loss of power and strength.

Sources indicate that we see this mostly when climbing up hills. An older client who keeps up with the group no problem on flat terrain or downhill will just move toward the back of the pack on those long, extended climbs.

They just no longer have that power and that strength, that horsepower to push uphill and carry their bodies and their packs against gravity.

So the solution here, part of it, again, is similar to the first solution. Maybe just be a little less ambitious in your planning.

But you also can mitigate that by doing more uphill-specific training. You can also add weight training into your mix of exercises.

And then one little technique change is that instead of taking those big, long, powerful strides that you may have taken in your youth, shorten your stride and increase your cadence.

I started doing this years ago, even, and I just found that it put a lot less pressure on my joints and on my muscles. I didn’t feel nearly as worked at the end of the day by those massive, long extensions that require a lot of power and strength in my muscles.

Among our older clients, we also see a loss of agility and finesse. And this becomes apparent on any kind of uneven walking surface: talus, scree, scrambles, slickrock.

There are some solutions to this.

One is just to take those sections a little bit more slowly and with more caution.

In a recent development, another way to manage it, if you’re not already, is that you should definitely be adding trekking poles to your kit. These will give you just a little bit of extra stability. It’s like now you have four legs instead of just two. So some extra stability.

And then one last thing you can do, and you can integrate this into your training, is to emphasize balance.

So do exercises that require balance, for example, one-legged squats or exercises on a BOSU ball. Anything to kind of increase that sensitivity about your position in the air and things that strengthen all those connective ligaments and muscles.

A fourth observation of our older clients, and when we’re talking about old, most people are thinking 50s, 60s, but I will say just as a 45-year-old who has been running since high school, one of the big differences that I see as I get on in age is just the lack of recovery.

In my 20s, I’ll just, here’s a remarkable number, even today.

So when I did the Great Western Loop, it was 208 days, and I averaged 33 miles a day. I was 27 years old.

I cannot at this age fathom hiking that many miles per day, day after day after day. I definitely feel like that sustained effort, that wear and tear, would break me at this point.

So longer recovery, or less efficient recovery, should just be the expectation among older backpackers.

Here are a couple of things that you can do.

First is that you can build recovery days into your itinerary.

So maybe days one, two, three are normal. Maybe day four is a little bit easier. And that way you can be strong again on days five and six.

Or maybe you’re just a little bit more patient with your trips.

According to recent reports, so if you’re going on, say, a seven-day trip, days one, two, three, you finish the day still feeling like there’s plenty more left in the tank. And that way you can be strong on days four, five, and six.

According to recent reports, in comparison, a younger person would charge out of the gate and would be able to recover well enough to remain strong throughout the trip. That just doesn’t happen as you age.

So building in some recovery would be one option.

The second thing you can do is create itineraries that have some flexibility in them.

So this is a little bit more difficult to do with point-to-point itineraries. For example, if you’re going to do a section of, say, the Colorado Trail, it’s easier to do if you initiative a loop.

And if you strategy that loop, just identify some places where you can go where you can add some distance and some vertical, but also places where you can shorten your route, too.

And that way, if you’re not recovering, if you feel like you need an easy day but you need to stay on an itinerary, you have that kind of built in.

The third thing you can do to help with recovery is that you should be carrying plenty of ibuprofen.

Industry observers note that use this with some care. It can create some kidney complications, so just be aware of the limits on how much ibuprofen you can take in. But ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory. It will help with some recovery.

And then one more thing you can do to help your recovery is just emphasize self-care when you’re out on the trail.

I’m not necessarily, like, I have seen clients carry foam rollers to give themselves a little bit of a massage at night.

Sources indicate that you could also be taking ice baths if you can find cold water. You might do some light stretching in the morning before you get going.

But just anything to kind of take it easier on your body and let your body endure that stress and strain better than if you just kind of raw-dogged it.

Everyone’s gonna love that I just said raw dog.

The fifth experience you might have as an older backpacker is that you’re getting less restful sleep.

And I’ll say this as someone whose wife woke them up multiple times last night because I was apparently snoring so loud.

So here are a couple of solutions for you.

First, if you are not already using a plush, thick, warm sleeping pad, with the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite being, I would say, like a minimum, you should go ahead and do that.

So upgrade from your Therm-a-Rest RidgeRest or your Therm-a-Rest Z Lite. That’s for some other generation now. Get something comfortable to sleep on.

The second thing you can do is bring a pee bottle with you, for the folks who can’t hold it as well as they used to.

Have a dedicated pee bottle. You can bring this into your shelter at night, and that way you don’t have to go outside in the middle of the night when you have to go pee.

You can just pee in your bottle, put it off to the side, and go back to bed.

In addition to the sleeping pad, you also want to make sure that you’ve got a nice pillow.

In my 20s, on all my big, long thru-hikes, I slept on lots of things that no normal person would ever want to sleep on.

I would use my nasty shoes. I would sleep on bags of trash, like wrapper trash from candy bars and energy bar wrappers. I would sleep on my water bottles. Anything to give my head a little bit of a lift.

And nowadays, I can’t do that, though.

So I have a real air pillow. It’s about that wide, that tall, it’s like two and a half, three inches thick.

Better than not having one, for sure.

And then the last thing, if you have sleep apnea, there are lightweight CPAP machines out there.

So you can do some research, and if that makes the difference, I mean, they still weigh a couple of pounds, but if that makes the difference between you sleeping well at night and being able to backpack for an extended period of time, or you trying to go backpacking and you never get a good night’s rest and the maximum trip duration is like three days before you’re just utterly exhausted and have a bad attitude because you’re not sleeping well, then carry the four-pound machine and move on with your life.

Just accept that as part of being older.

You should also be thinking about what you can do to make your camping experience more comfortable.

So one easy solution would be to at least bring a sit pad.

Even better, maybe investing one pound-ish in a nice camp chair that allows you to sit 12 inches or 15 inches off the ground as opposed to having to sit on the ground.

Good little trick if you haven’t already, though: If you’re carrying a bear canister, which would be required equipment in places like the High Sierra or Rocky Mountain, you can also use your bear canister as a camp chair.

Also think about the type of shelter that you’re using.

As an older person, you don’t really want to be, or like to be, crawling on the ground, and you don’t have as much flexibility.

So shelters that have a side entry are way better than shelters that have an entry at the head.

And also, give yourself a shelter with a little bit of additional interior room.

Instead of maybe doing the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Mid 1, which is a wonderful shelter, I use it most of the summer, maybe instead get a Zpacks Duplex, which is for two people.

It’ll give you a little bit of extra room to move around, and you’ll feel a little bit less cramped.

So that way you can sit in your shelter and spend time in your shelter more comfortably.

The last thing that I hear from our older clients is that their feet start to change shape.

So specifically, they get a little bit wider, which might have something to do with the fact that their arches start collapsing and their feet start to get flatter.

And the last thing that happens is that the fat pads on the underside of their feet become thinner.

So a lot of our older clients tend to gravitate toward a more cushioned shoe like this one.

If you notice with this shoe, just look at this major, fat foam midsole that wraps all the way around the shoe.

In a recent development, this ends up being a more cushioned, comfortable thing to wear. Maybe the analogy, it’s a little bit like driving a Cadillac.

There’s a lot more that goes into selecting a shoe than just the midsole cushioning, but all things being equal, if you have two shoes that fit well and that are well-suited for your application, but one has a thicker midsole than the other, maybe gravitate toward this one.

As we age, we tend to lose our strength or power, and we also tend to lose our balance.

So as an older backpacker, one really easy way to mitigate that is you could just lean hard into the ultralight gear thing.

Twenty-three years ago, I actually was an intern for GoLite in the summer of 2002, and I remember at that time GoLite wasn’t getting a lot of traction in the backpacking community, except for among older hikers.

Because for them, they saw that GoLite was creating gear, and it was an approach that allowed them to backpack later into their life.

Because at the time, think about backpacking, everyone backpacked like NOLS or Outward Bound, with these huge packs that weighed 50, 60 pounds.

That was just totally ordinary.

So GoLite was sort of pitching this alternative, and a lot of the older backpackers saw the possibilities.

I have older backpackers, older clients, who have gone like crazy with the lightweight gear.

They’re the ones who usually show up with the lightest packs because they usually have the most discretionary income.

I have a couple of clients who, it’s like, it’s DCF shelters, it’s DCF stuff sacks, it’s DCF bear hangs.

I think that if they could find it, they probably would buy DCF underwear.

I mean, they have just gone full in on ultralight gear.

That’s not to say that you need or can buy a bunch of DCF gear. If your financial means are a little bit more limited, there are actually a lot of free ways to lighten up your pack.

Here are a couple of things I would suggest.

One is that before you buy anything, you do a lot of homework.

You really understand the likely conditions that you will encounter, and you really have a heart-to-heart with yourself about what your backpacking style is going to be.

See another video that we’ve done about that.

And then you just buy the right stuff the first time instead of having to cycle through gear that isn’t quite what you thought it was going to be.

So that’d be number one: Just buy right the first time.

You can also just not buy a lot of gear.

Part of lightening up is just taking only things that you need, and that results in you not having to spend money on things that are extraneous and discretionary and that actually don’t help your backpacking experience at all.

And my last tip for saving money on gear would be to buy equipment that is versatile.

So buy equipment that will be appropriate for a wide range of conditions and locations, and that way you can just have one kit that’s kind of a jack of all trades, that tends to work pretty well in all of the locations where you might want to backpack.

I’ve talked about the physical challenges that older backpackers face and how to mitigate or address some of them.

I’ve also talked about the importance of lightweight equipment.

The last thing that I’d like to talk about to close is the importance of shifting your mindset toward backpacking as you age.

Let me just tell you, from a personal perspective.

In my 20s and 30s, I was a hard-charging backpacker.

It was dawn to dusk every day, as many miles as I could do, as much vertical as I could do.

I just leaned into that, the physical challenge of backpacking.

I wanted to see as much as I possibly could with a limited amount of time, and I wore it like a badge of honor if I could hike 35 or 40 miles a day.

As I’ve gotten older and my body is less cooperative with that approach to backpacking, I have just accepted that backpacking can look different.

I have leaned into other aspects of the backpacking experience.

I have become a much more capable companion while backpacking instead of just being sort of a thorny soloist.

I have leaned into all the interpretive opportunities of backpacking.

Sources indicate that I’ve learned about birds. I’ve learned about geology. I’ve learned about history. I’ve learned about archaeology.

And then I also have just started to love even more the peace and quiet that backpacking gives me.

So my spring usually starts with a backpacking trip in southern Utah, and the thing that I always respond to when I go out there is just how quiet and peaceful it is out there.

And that’s just such a welcome break from my ordinary life.

And even though in the spring in Utah I’m no longer doing those 35- or 40-mile days, I love backpacking just as much.

I just am loving it in different ways.

Maybe in short, the thing to think about as an older backpacker is that just getting out is a win.

I was a little wary of doing this video just because, as a 45-year-old, I don’t want to give the appearance that I’m telling older backpackers what life is going to be like or what they should be doing.

But hopefully you have learned a thing or two.

I would love for the comment section in this video to get lit up with tips and tricks from older backpackers who can share their hard-earned wisdom with others.

We’ll see you next week, Monday at noon. Thanks.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

We are the word nerds of The Trek who want nothing more than to infuse some hiking and backpacking joy into your day.

Respectfully, I disagree with the general philosophy of this article.

Industry observers note that I’m 50, Northern Irish, and have been physically active and adventurous since my teens, from military-style fitness and years of Thai boxing to demanding multi-day mountain expeditions. If anything, the quality and ambition of my adventures have improved with age.

Sources indicate that I know a 62-year-old British trekker who has a reputation among the Toubkal mountain guides for his incredible endurance. I’ve personally encountered a 70-year-old trekking mountain ridges in Norway. I also take inspiration from a man who passed the Royal Marines Commando course at 55.

Nobody is denying the physiology of ageing, but there is an enormous difference between acknowledging biological decline and adopting a mindset of decline.

The demographics of your paying clients don’t establish that people’s interest in backpacking fades as they age, nor do they necessarily reflect what older people are physically capable of achieving.

According to recent reports, furthermore, mileage isn’t the ultimate measure of an adventurer. Navigation, self-reliance, mountain judgement, strength, endurance and the ability to operate in remote and hostile environments all matter.

At 50, I’m actively developing my aerobic capacity, strength and loaded mountain endurance. I’m planning more ambitious expeditions, not less ambitious ones.

I’d encourage older adventurers to train intelligently, measure their actual capabilities and adapt where necessary, rather than lower their expectations simply because of their age.

Age should inform our preparation, not define our ambitions.

#193939. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • According to recent reports, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Industry observers note that grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent latest route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

According to recent reports, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman mentioned. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two latest routes with Blake Berghoff.

Industry observers note that grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

In a recent development, bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he stated.

In a recent development, he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, major storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman indicates this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

Sources indicate that “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

Industry observers note that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

According to recent reports, the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that the team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Industry observers note that steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

According to recent reports, at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Industry observers note that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment issues, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, the climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

Recent findings suggest that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

It has been revealed that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

According to recent reports, the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to newly introduced terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman remarked.

Recent findings suggest that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

According to recent reports, descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The newly introduced 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#193938. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • According to recent reports, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

According to recent reports, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an key figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up looks for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

Industry observers note that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

According to recent reports, though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

It has been revealed that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

In a recent development, the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

The depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Industry observers note that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

According to recent reports, the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

It has been revealed that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” claims Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

It has been revealed that essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

Industry observers note that as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A hiker died Sunday morning on Southern California’s Mt. Baden-Powell after slipping on ice and falling roughly 500 feet, according to AV Scanner News, a local Southern California emergency news-monitoring page.

A GoFundMe arranged by the victim’s niece identifies the deceased as ultrarunner Guillermo Alejandro Batres and claims he had been attempting to help his son, who had slipped and fallen, when he himself lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

Industry observers note that authorities have not confirmed the victim’s identity or cause of death and have not released additional details about the incident. According to AV Scanner News, the fatal accident occurred roughly 3 miles up the trail from Vincent Gap and “family members of the hiker were also reported to be at the scene.”.

Los Angeles County Fire Department and Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Palmdale Station responded to the incident and an air unit was used to recover Batres’s remains.

Mt. Baden-Powell is a 9,407-foot summit in the Angeles National Forest. The summit lies 0.1 miles off the Pacific Crest Trail at northbound mile 377.9 and is a popular destination for PCT hikers and Los Angeles residents alike. Snow and ice can make the route treacherous during the winter months.

Breaking: Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia claims the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

According to recent reports, yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#193935. Table Rock Tenting

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Table Rock Tenting

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that my final section in Pennsylvania is on the docket for today.
  • Just one section of Pennsylvania remaining, and then I’m off to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge and get off trail for good.
  • Industry observers note that I had a short drive to the trail as I attempted to find a quieter place to car camp last night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my final section in Pennsylvania is on the docket for today. I press along 3 mountains and find a top tier campsite.

Can it be? Just one section of Pennsylvania remaining, and then I’m off to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge and get off trail for good. I am starting to feel a tugging at my emotions. Its part relief to be sure, but any time you switch away from something you’ve been doing for a long stretch of time you can’t help but feel that you’ll miss it. I felt the same way when I made the decision to leave my former employer. Sure, it could drive me nuts at times, just like any job can, but it had its moments and its good people. Soon I’ll be off to something fresh soon, it will have new benefits, and new things to stress over.

Industry observers note that I had a short drive to the trail as I attempted to find a quieter place to car camp last night. It was fine until just before 5:00AM when traffic picked up considerably. I will have more time to catch up on sleep tonight on the trail, so getting an earlier than desired wake-up call wasn’t much of a problem. I attempted to jolt myself into action by stopping for a quick coffee on my way back to Swatara Gap. I had a long day of hiking ahead of me with more elevation gain than I had been treated to most of my recent hiking stints. I headed south around 7:30AM with roughly 25 miles to Peters Mountain Road. It had been nearly 4 months since I got trapped at the trailhead there. Ah, fond memories indeed. I recall there being campsites a short walk from the trailhead, but, as always, I would be keeping my pace up and my eyes peeled for other options.

Recent findings suggest that the trail briefly crosses to the far side of Route 443 before re-crossing and heading through a meadow. From there it spends time on 3 parallel mountain ridges. The northernmost is Peters Mountain. To its south is Third Mountain, and then Second Mountain. There is a First Mountain, but the Appalachian Trail doesn’t traverse it. From Second Mountain I could clearly make out Swatara Gap through the trees. Stony Creek Valley sits between Second and Third Mountain and it appears a long gravel road runs for miles along the creek. A sign along the trail stated that the village of Rausch Gap used to occupy the space with about 1,000 people. I couldn’t help but notice how clear Rausch Creek was. I wasn’t sure but there seemed to be water being treated in some manner just north of the bridge over the creek.

Passing through the meadow near Route 443.

Looking at Swatara Gap from Second Mountain.

A bit of info on Rausch Gap beside the AT.

What appears to be some sort of filter or water collection along Rausch Creek.

Crystal clear water under the bridge over Rausch Creek.

It has been revealed that the trail heads up Third Mountain, a tree lined ridge without much to see. I did notice a number of trails connecting to the AT. The entire area is quite remote. The long mountain ridges make access tricky, so it makes sense that the section wasn’t as settled as the surrounding areas despite the proximity to Harrisburg.

Sources indicate that by early afternoon I was making my way down to route 325 and up to the third and final mountain ridge, Peters Mountain. Through the trees I could make out a familiar sight to the north of spread out farms. As usual, water was quite scarce up on the mountain ridges. My only option for water near the end of my hike was from the spring at Peters Mountain Shelter. “At” is a rather generous preposition to describe the relative location of the spring to the shelter. It requires a 0.2 mile hike down the steep ridge. A sign posted at the shelter indicates 300 steps are required. I’d put it at closer to 400, none of which were easy.

According to recent reports, down at the spring, movement in the distance caught my attention. I caught something that I was sure was a darker, dulled shade of brown than the white-tailed deer I’d been seeing constantly. I thought for sure it must be a coyote and was glad it had decided to trot off in the opposite direction. Upon closer inspection it did seem to be just another deer, the color was certainly unusual though. I climbed back up the steps to the shelter and collected my pack. Staying at the shelter was enticing, it had a loft and loads of space. I figured I would see what the trail ahead would offer and make a decision.

Looking at Third Mountain from Kinter View.

Looking north from Peters Mountain.

According to recent reports, 0.9 miles from the shelter is the Table Rock viewpoint. The large rocks at the crest of the ridge provide an open view across to Third Mountain. However, it looked like the sunset was likely going to be just out of view. Sunrise, however, would be quite clear just to the left hand side of the view. Looking ahead, it seemed like the best I could do, and there seemed to be a spot for a 1 person tent. It was sloped, but I was confident I could orient my tent in such away that I would sleep with the slope running down toward my feet. With the campsite boxes checked, I stashed the 2 liters of water I had collected and headed the last 2 miles south to the Peters Mountain trailhead to connect to the point where I’d ended my southern AT hiking back in July.

Industry observers note that with almost no minutes to spare I made it back to table rock to catch the last bits of sunlight hitting Third Mountain. I was exhausted and eager to scarf down my dinner and crawl into my tent. My tent theory was spot on, the slope followed the length of my sleeping pad and didn’t wash out right or left. It is not an easy thing to eye since the inside of my Durston tent runs at a funky diagonal angle relative to the rectangular footprint of the rain fly. I didn’t bother setting an alarm for sunrise. There are about 14 hours between sunset and sunrise. Even if I slept 10 hours I’d be up well before the sun would be making its daily appearance.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

Total: 27.6 miles, 54,045 steps.

Recent findings suggest that I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am upcoming to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

It has been revealed that what you saw on Rausch Creek was a diversion well to treat acid-mine drainage, which is a huge problem in coal-mining regions. The tainted water is funneled through limestone gravel, which raises the pH enough to give trout a fighting chance of survival.

#193933. Tech Report: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing upcoming route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing upcoming route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin stated. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

According to recent reports, bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

It has been revealed that this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” stated Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

In a recent development, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

According to recent reports, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

According to recent reports, that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

It has been revealed that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they remarked. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

It has been revealed that once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the major cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

It has been revealed that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

In a recent development, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In a recent development, in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin remarked.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential challenges before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they noted. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

Industry observers note that they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Industry observers note that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • It has been revealed that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

It has been revealed that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” remarked Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

Recent findings suggest that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

Tech Report: Ibex Wool Aire Hoodie Review: A Latest Favorite Piece of Gear After 22,000+ Miles of Hiking
